title: The promotion nobody warned you about
summary: Traffic goes from 600 to 9,000 req/s in one step, and your instances take a minute to start.

statement.situation: Marketing sent a push notification to every user without telling engineering. Normal traffic is around 600 requests/s; within seconds it jumps to 9,000 and stays there for several minutes. Your service has autoscaling, but new instances take about a minute to become useful, and the mobile client retries failed requests twice.
symptoms: Latency climbs, then requests time out
Retries pile more load on top of the spike
The database runs out of connections while servers are still starting
requirements: Keep the product working through the surge — most requests must succeed
No cascading failure: the system must not collapse and stay down after the spike
Retries must not multiply the load beyond control
constraints: You cannot change the client's retry behaviour
You cannot pre-warm for a spike you weren't told about (assume nothing changes before it starts)

learningObjectives: Offloading work instead of only adding capacity

references.title: Google SRE book: Addressing cascading failures
AWS Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload

scenarios.name: Push-notification spike
scenarios.description: 600 → 9,000 req/s at t=30 s, held for 4 minutes. Requests that take over 1.5 s count as failed.

successCriteria.label: Most requests succeed once the spike is underway (≥ 85%)
Steady state restored soon after capacity arrives
